Every command in this guide is run from projects/01-cost-visibility/ unless the command says otherwise. Terraform files live in terraform/ inside that folder. Check progress any time with ./scripts/check.sh — it never touches Azure and never costs anything.

How it fits together

Fourteen resources, but only three paths through them. An alerting path that ends at a human, a data path that ends at a dashboard, and an identity that is allowed to read the bill and nothing else.

Solid lines carry data. Dashed lines are permission and delivery. Everything left of the storage account is built by Terraform; the workbook tiles get added in the portal in phase 11.

Why the forecast alert is the one that matters

Most people set a budget alert at 100% and stop. That alert tells you the money is already gone. A forecast alert watches the slope instead of the total, so it fires while there is still a month left to do something about it.

Same spending, two alerts. The actual-spend alert is correct and useless; by the time it fires the budget is spent.

0.0

How to read these tasks

Every Terraform task in this lab is the same shape. Learn it once here and the other eleven are the same job with different words.

Why it mattersThe point of this page is that you stop needing step-by-step direction. Once the pattern is in your head, a task like "create a storage account with versioning" is enough.
PartWhat it means
resourceThe keyword. You are declaring a thing that should exist.
"azurerm_resource_group"The type. Comes from the provider. Never invented — always looked up.
"main"The local name. Yours to pick. Only used to reference it elsewhere in your own code.
{ ... }The arguments. Which ones exist, and which are required, is in the docs for that type.
Where everything lives. All Terraform for this lab goes in projects/01-cost-visibility/terraform/. One file per concern: main.tf (foundation, identity, storage), monitoring.tf (alerts), budget.tf, export.tf, outputs.tf. Terraform reads every .tf file in the folder and treats them as one config, so the split is purely for humans. Write each task where its TODO marker already sits.
How do I find the arguments?

Go to <a href="https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/azurerm/latest/docs" target="_blank">the azurerm provider docs</a>. Use the search box on the left. Type the resource type, for example <code>resource_group</code>. Open it. Two sections matter: <b>Example Usage</b>, which is copyable shape, and <b>Argument Reference</b>, which tells you what is Required versus Optional. Required arguments are the only ones you strictly need; the rest are choices you are making on purpose.

How do I point one resource at another?

Use <code>type.local_name.attribute</code>. So the resource group you declare as <code>resource "azurerm_resource_group" "main"</code> is referenced elsewhere as <code>azurerm_resource_group.main.name</code> or <code>.location</code> or <code>.id</code>.

This matters for more than typing. Referencing is how Terraform learns the order to build things in. If you hardcode the string <code>"rg-costvis"</code> instead, Terraform has no idea the two are related and may try to build them in the wrong order.

Which attributes exist is listed under <b>Attributes Reference</b> on each docs page.

What is the loop?

Write a block, then run <code>./scripts/check.sh</code>. It shows remaining TODOs, runs <code>terraform fmt</code>, and runs <code>terraform validate</code>. Nothing touches Azure and nothing costs money, so run it as often as you like.

Validate catches wrong argument names, missing required arguments, and type errors. It does not catch a value that is legal but wrong, which is what the requirement checks at the end are for.

Expect validation to fail until the last task is done, because <code>workbook.tf</code> references resources you have not written yet. That is normal.

What if I get stuck?

In order: read the error, since Terraform names the file, line, and usually the exact argument. Then check the docs page for that resource. Then open the Level 1 hint on the task. Then use the tutor button on the step, which can read your actual file and tell you what is wrong.

Asking the tutor is not cheating. Opening Level 3 and copying the code without understanding it is the only thing that defeats the purpose.

Foundation

Open terraform/main.tf and work top to bottom. Terraform in one sentence: you describe what you want, and it makes Azure match.
1.1

Resource group

Write it interraform/main.tf replacing# TODO 1.1

A folder. Everything in this lab goes inside it, and deleting the folder deletes everything in it.

Real lifeThis is exactly why cloud bills spiral. People create things in random places, forget them, and pay for years. One folder per project means one command cleans it all up.
Why it mattersTags are how you answer 'what did this project cost?'. Untagged resources are the reason companies can't attribute their own spending.
What to set on azurerm_resource_group
  • name — "rg-${var.name_prefix}", which gives rg-costvis
  • location — var.location
  • tags — var.tags
Hint
Search azurerm_resource_group at the registry and open Example Usage. It needs three arguments and nothing more.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_resource_group" "main" {
  name     = "rg-${var.name_prefix}"
  location = var.location
  tags     = var.tags
}
1.2

Log Analytics workspace

Write it interraform/main.tf replacing# TODO 1.2

Where logs go so you can search them later. Without it, logs are written and thrown away.

Real lifeThis is what you'd search after an incident to answer 'who accessed that, and when?'. Here it records who read your cost data.
Why it mattersWriting azurerm_resource_group.main.name instead of the literal string tells Terraform this depends on that, so it builds them in the right order automatically.
What to set on azurerm_log_analytics_workspace
  • name — "law-${var.name_prefix}"
  • location and resource_group_name — reference the group from 1.1 rather than retyping it
  • sku — "PerGB2018" (first 5 GB/month ingested is free)
  • retention_in_days — var.log_retention_days
  • tags
Answer this in DECISIONS.md: retention defaults to 30 days, not the 730-day maximum. Why deliberately keep less?
Hint
Search azurerm_log_analytics_workspace. The SKU you want is the pay-as-you-go one, and retention is measured in days.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_log_analytics_workspace" "main" {
  name                = "law-${var.name_prefix}"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.main.location
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.main.name

  sku               = "PerGB2018"
  retention_in_days = var.log_retention_days

  tags = var.tags
}

P2

Identity and access

The security core of the lab.
1.3

Managed identity

Write it interraform/main.tf replacing# TODO 1.3

A login for software instead of a person. No password exists, so no password can leak.

Real lifeThe classic breach: a developer hardcodes a password, pushes it to GitHub, and a bot finds it within minutes. A managed identity removes the password entirely — Azure handles it invisibly.
What to set on azurerm_user_assigned_identity
  • name — "id-${var.name_prefix}-reader"
  • location, resource_group_name, tags
Hint
Search azurerm_user_assigned_identity. It takes the same four basics as the resource group plus a location.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_user_assigned_identity" "cost_reader" {
  name                = "id-${var.name_prefix}-reader"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.main.location
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.main.name
  tags                = var.tags
}
1.4

Role assignment — least privilege

Write it interraform/main.tf replacing# TODO 1.4

The identity above can currently do nothing at all. This grants it exactly one permission: read cost data.

Real lifeRansomware spreads because service accounts have far more access than they need. One over-permissioned backup account can end a company. Least privilege asks: if this is stolen, what's the worst that happens? Here the answer is 'someone learns what your bill was.'
Why it mattersA managed identity has two IDs. principal_id is who it is, used for permissions. client_id is how apps address it. Using the wrong one produces an error that doesn't explain itself.
What to set on azurerm_role_assignment
  • scope — data.azurerm_subscription.current.id. Billing lives at subscription level, not inside your resource group
  • role_definition_name — "Cost Management Reader"
  • principal_id — the identity's principal_id
Hint
Search azurerm_role_assignment. Three arguments: where the permission applies, which permission, and who gets it. Think about which of the identity's two IDs represents who it is.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_role_assignment" "cost_reader" {
  scope                = data.azurerm_subscription.current.id
  role_definition_name = "Cost Management Reader"
  principal_id         = azurerm_user_assigned_identity.cost_reader.principal_id
}
P3

Storage

'Misconfigured storage bucket' is one of the most common breach headlines there is. This phase is about not being that.
1.5

Storage account — the security baseline

Write it interraform/main.tf replacing# TODO 1.5

Cloud file storage. Your daily bill copies land here.

Real lifeMillions of records get exposed this way every year, always the same root cause: someone left a container public. Every setting below is a control that has prevented a real breach somewhere.
Why it mattersVersioning plus soft delete is ransomware defense. Ransomware encrypts files by overwriting them. With versioning on, the originals are still there.
What to set on azurerm_storage_account
  • name — "st${var.name_prefix}${random_string.suffix.result}". No hyphens allowed, and it must be globally unique across all of Azure
  • account_tier "Standard", account_replication_type "LRS", account_kind "StorageV2"
  • HTTPS-only traffic — no unencrypted connections
  • Minimum TLS 1.2 — blocks old, breakable encryption
  • Public access disabled — this is the headline one
  • A blob_properties block with versioning on and 7-day soft delete for both blobs and containers
Hint
Search azurerm_storage_account. The security arguments are near the top of the docs page; data protection lives inside a nested blob_properties block. One argument name changed in provider v4 — if you use the v3 name you'll get a clear error, so read it.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_storage_account" "exports" {
  name                = "st${var.name_prefix}${random_string.suffix.result}"
  location            = azurerm_resource_group.main.location
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.main.name

  account_tier             = "Standard"
  account_replication_type = "LRS"
  account_kind             = "StorageV2"

  https_traffic_only_enabled      = true
  min_tls_version                 = "TLS1_2"
  allow_nested_items_to_be_public = false

  blob_properties {
    versioning_enabled = true

    delete_retention_policy {
      days = 7
    }

    container_delete_retention_policy {
      days = 7
    }
  }

  tags = var.tags
}
1.6

Storage container

Write it interraform/main.tf replacing# TODO 1.6

A folder inside the storage account.

Real lifeprivate means nobody on the internet can read it without credentials. Older systems defaulted to public, which is precisely how those breaches happened.
What to set on azurerm_storage_container
  • name — "cost-exports"
  • storage_account_id — reference the account from 1.5
  • container_access_type — "private"
Hint
Search azurerm_storage_container. In provider v4 it takes the account by ID, not by name — that changed from v3.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_storage_container" "exports" {
  name                  = "cost-exports"
  storage_account_id    = azurerm_storage_account.exports.id
  container_access_type = "private"
}
1.7

Diagnostic settings

Write it interraform/main.tf replacing# TODO 1.7

Turns on logging for the storage account and sends it to the workspace from 1.2.

Real lifeAfter any breach the first question is 'what did they access?'. Without this there is no answer. Cost data is sensitive — it reveals what systems you run and how big you are.
Why it mattersUse enabled_metric, not metric. The old name is deprecated and disappears in the next major provider version.
What to set on azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting
  • target_resource_id — the account ID with "/blobServices/default" appended. The blob service, not the account
  • log_analytics_workspace_id — the workspace from 1.2
  • Three log categories: StorageRead, StorageWrite, StorageDelete
  • One metric category: Transaction
Hint
Search azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting. Log categories are repeated blocks, one per category.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting" "storage_blob" {
  name                       = "diag-blob"
  target_resource_id         = "${azurerm_storage_account.exports.id}/blobServices/default"
  log_analytics_workspace_id = azurerm_log_analytics_workspace.main.id

  enabled_log {
    category = "StorageRead"
  }

  enabled_log {
    category = "StorageWrite"
  }

  enabled_log {
    category = "StorageDelete"
  }

  enabled_metric {
    category = "Transaction"
  }
}
P4

Alerts

Open terraform/monitoring.tf.
2.1

Action group

Write it interraform/monitoring.tf replacing# TODO 2.1

The delivery list. Alerts don't send themselves — they hand off to an action group, which emails, texts, or calls.

Real lifeWhen you need to add your manager to every alert, you change one action group instead of editing every rule and forgetting two.
Why it mattersvar.alert_emails is a list. A single hardcoded block only handles one address — you need Terraform's dynamic blocks, which generate one block per list item.
What to set on azurerm_monitor_action_group
  • name, resource_group_name, and short_name — "costalert" (max 12 chars; Azure uses it as an SMS prefix)
  • One email receiver per address in var.alert_emails, each with the common alert schema enabled
Hint
Search azurerm_monitor_action_group, then look up dynamic blocks. Inside a dynamic block named email_receiver, the iterator is also called email_receiver, with .key and .value.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_monitor_action_group" "cost" {
  name                = "ag-${var.name_prefix}"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.main.name
  short_name          = "costalert"

  dynamic "email_receiver" {
    for_each = var.alert_emails

    content {
      name                    = "email-${email_receiver.key}"
      email_address           = email_receiver.value
      use_common_alert_schema = true
    }
  }

  tags = var.tags
}
2.2

Cost anomaly alert

Write it interraform/monitoring.tf replacing# TODO 2.2

Azure learns your normal daily spend and tells you when today doesn't match.

Real lifeA monthly budget is slow. If something starts costing $200/day on the 3rd, the budget stays silent until the running total crosses a threshold — maybe two weeks and $2,800 later. The anomaly alert catches the shape changing the next day.
What to set on azurerm_cost_anomaly_alert
  • name, display_name, subscription_id
  • email_subject, email_addresses, message
Hint
Search "cost anomaly" at the registry. This one emails directly rather than going through an action group.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_cost_anomaly_alert" "main" {
  name            = "anomaly-${var.name_prefix}"
  display_name    = "Daily cost anomaly"
  subscription_id = data.azurerm_subscription.current.id
  email_subject   = "Azure cost anomaly detected"
  email_addresses = var.alert_emails
  message         = "Daily spend deviated from the learned pattern. Check Cost Analysis for the responsible resource."
}
P5

The budget

Open terraform/budget.tf. This is the centrepiece — get the threshold design right and the rest is plumbing.
3.1

Subscription budget

Write it interraform/budget.tf replacing# TODO 3.1

A spending limit that emails you as you approach it.

Why it mattersEach notification needs enabled, threshold, operator, threshold_type, contact_emails, and contact_groups pointing at the action group from 2.1.
What to set on azurerm_consumption_budget_subscription
  • name, subscription_id — the full resource ID, not a bare GUID
  • amount from var.monthly_budget, time_grain monthly
  • A time_period block using the two date variables
  • Four notification blocks — see the table below
thresholdthreshold_typeWhat it means
50ActualHalf the budget is gone
80ActualGetting close — go look
100ActualBudget is gone
100ForecastedOn pace to blow it
This table is the whole lab. The first three are history — they tell you money is already spent. The fourth is a warning that arrives while you can still act. When an interviewer asks what you'd do differently from a default setup, this is the answer.
Hint
Search azurerm_consumption_budget_subscription. Notifications are repeated blocks — four of them. The operator is the same for all four.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_consumption_budget_subscription" "main" {
  name            = "budget-${var.name_prefix}"
  subscription_id = data.azurerm_subscription.current.id

  amount     = var.monthly_budget
  time_grain = "Monthly"

  time_period {
    start_date = var.budget_start_date
    end_date   = var.budget_end_date
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 50.0
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Actual"
    contact_emails = var.alert_emails
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.cost.id]
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 80.0
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Actual"
    contact_emails = var.alert_emails
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.cost.id]
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 100.0
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Actual"
    contact_emails = var.alert_emails
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.cost.id]
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 100.0
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Forecasted"
    contact_emails = var.alert_emails
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.cost.id]
  }
}
P6

Export and outputs

4.1

Daily cost export

Write it interraform/export.tf replacing# TODO 4.1

Azure writes a CSV of your real usage into storage every day.

Real lifeThe portal is fine for 'what am I spending now'. It's useless for 'what did this look like in March' once the view resets. The export is your own permanent copy.
Why it mattersTerraform normally works out order by watching which resources reference each other. This export never mentions the role assignment, so Terraform doesn't know it must wait for permissions — and would happily create an export that silently fails its first run. You have to say it out loud.
What to set on azurerm_subscription_cost_management_export
  • name, subscription_id, daily recurrence, and the two period dates
  • An export_data_storage_location block pointing at the container from 1.6, with root_folder_path = "daily"
  • export_data_options with type = "ActualCost" and time_frame = "MonthToDate"
  • depends_on the role assignment from 1.4
Hint
Search azurerm_subscription_cost_management_export. Two nested blocks: where it writes, and what it writes. ActualCost is what was billed; AmortizedCost spreads reservation purchases over time.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
resource "azurerm_subscription_cost_management_export" "daily" {
  name                         = "export-${var.name_prefix}-daily"
  subscription_id              = data.azurerm_subscription.current.id
  recurrence_type              = "Daily"
  recurrence_period_start_date = var.budget_start_date
  recurrence_period_end_date   = var.budget_end_date

  export_data_storage_location {
    container_id     = azurerm_storage_container.exports.id
    root_folder_path = "daily"
  }

  export_data_options {
    type = "ActualCost"

    time_frame = "MonthToDate"
  }

  depends_on = [azurerm_role_assignment.cost_reader]
}
5.1

Outputs

Write it interraform/outputs.tf replacing# TODO 5.1

Print the things you'd otherwise go hunting in the portal for.

Why it mattersTerraform doesn't require descriptions. Anyone reading your code in six months does.
What to set
  • Resource group name, storage account name, budget name, the identity's client ID
  • Each needs a description
Hint
An output block is output "name" { value = ... description = "..." }. Reference resources the same way you did inside them.
Reference solution — try it yourself first
output "resource_group" {
  description = "Resource group holding everything in this project."
  value       = azurerm_resource_group.main.name
}

output "storage_account" {
  description = "Storage account receiving the daily cost export."
  value       = azurerm_storage_account.exports.name
}

output "workbook_url" {
  description = "Direct link to the cost dashboard in the Azure portal."
  value       = "https://portal.azure.com/#@/resource${azurerm_application_insights_workbook.cost.id}/workbook"
}

output "budget_name" {
  description = "Name of the subscription budget."
  value       = azurerm_consumption_budget_subscription.main.name
}

output "cost_reader_client_id" {
  description = "Client ID of the least-privilege identity used to read cost data."
  value       = azurerm_user_assigned_identity.cost_reader.client_id
}

output "monthly_budget_usd" {
  description = "Budget the alert thresholds are calculated against."
  value       = var.monthly_budget
}

P9

Prove the control works

The most important phase, and the one almost nobody does.
9.1

Test that least privilege denies

Sign in as the managed identity and try something outside its role. It must fail. Then read cost data, which must succeed.

Real lifeThis is what a security audit actually asks for. Not 'is MFA enabled' but 'show me a login being blocked'. Evidence beats configuration.
Tell me when you reach this step and I'll give you the exact commands. They depend on values from your apply outputs.
Screenshot
rbac-denied — Terminal showing AuthorizationFailed when the identity attempts a write.
./scripts/capture.sh rbac-denied "Identity denied when attempting an action outside its role"
Screenshot
rbac-allowed — Terminal showing the same identity successfully reading cost data.
